title: Medicare Part B Copay Elimination ACO: 2027 Changes

sections.text: What This New CMS Rule Actually Means for You

sections.content: Starting in April 2027, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) will allow certain Medicare Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) to waive the Part B coinsurance you normally pay for primary care office visits. That 20% coinsurance has long applied after you meet your Part B deductible, and this change would let qualifying ACOs reduce or eliminate it for covered primary care services.

This waiver is not automatic for every Medicare beneficiary. It only applies if your doctor's practice participates in an ACO that chooses to offer it. Your Part B premium and annual deductible still apply no matter what; the waiver only affects the coinsurance portion tied to qualifying office visits.

sections.calloutText: The 2026 Part B deductible is $283 and the standard monthly premium is $202.90. Neither of these changes under the new ACO copay waiver; only the 20% coinsurance on qualifying primary care visits is affected.

sections.text: Why Medicare Terms Like ACO Can Feel Confusing

sections.content: An Accountable Care Organization, or ACO, is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other healthcare providers who voluntarily work together under Medicare to coordinate your care. The goal is better communication between your providers and fewer unnecessary tests or duplicated services, not a separate insurance plan you choose.

ACOs are often confused with Medicare Advantage plans, but the two are different. Medicare Advantage is a private plan that replaces your Original Medicare coverage, with its own network and cost structure. An ACO, by contrast, operates within Original Medicare. You can remain on Original Medicare, keep any Medigap policy you have, and still be connected to an ACO through your doctor's participation.

Because of this, being part of an ACO does not change your plan type, your card, or how you access care. The only thing that changes is how Medicare pays your doctor behind the scenes, and now, potentially, whether your coinsurance gets waived for certain visits.

sections.text: How You Get Assigned to an ACO

sections.content: You do not sign up for an ACO directly. CMS assigns, or "attributes," beneficiaries to an ACO based on which doctor provides most of their primary care, determined by reviewing claims history over time.

items: CMS reviews your claims history to see which primary care provider you visit most often.
CMS identifies whether that provider participates in an ACO.
If you're attributed to an ACO, you typically receive a notification letter explaining the arrangement.

sections.content: If you want to know sooner, you can simply ask your doctor's office whether their practice participates in an ACO. Office staff or billing departments usually know this information and can tell you directly.

sections.text: How the Copay Waiver Could Lower Your Out-of-Pocket Costs

sections.content: To see how this could affect your wallet, consider a hypothetical example. Say a primary care office visit is billed at $150 after you've met your Part B deductible. Under standard Part B cost-sharing, you'd typically owe 20% coinsurance, or $30, while Medicare covers the rest. Under a qualifying ACO's copay waiver, that $30 coinsurance could be eliminated entirely for that visit, leaving you with no out-of-pocket cost for the office visit itself.

This adds up for people who see their primary care doctor often, such as those managing diabetes, high blood pressure, or other conditions that require regular monitoring. A handful of $30 or $40 coinsurance charges across a year is a meaningful amount for many retirees on fixed incomes.

It's worth being clear about the limits of this waiver. It applies specifically to Part B-covered primary care office visits within a qualifying ACO; it does not extend to specialist visits, hospital outpatient services, diagnostic procedures, or other Part B services outside that scope. Those services continue to carry their normal coinsurance under Original Medicare.

If you have frequent primary care visits and no Medigap plan covering your Part B coinsurance, this waiver is worth tracking closely as April 2027 approaches. I'd suggest confirming your doctor's ACO status now, so you're not caught guessing when the rule takes effect.

sections.text: Who Stands to Benefit Most From This Change

sections.content: The copay waiver will matter more to some beneficiaries than others, depending on how often they see a primary care doctor and what other coverage they already have.

items: Beneficiaries with chronic conditions that require frequent primary care visits, since recurring coinsurance charges add up over a year.
Those without supplemental coverage like Medigap, who currently pay the 20% coinsurance out of pocket on every visit.
Lower-income seniors who are sensitive to recurring copays, even relatively small ones, as part of a fixed monthly budget.
Caregivers managing healthcare costs for a parent or loved one, who may see a direct reduction in what they help cover.

sections.content: If you already have a Medigap plan that covers Part B coinsurance, such as Plan G or Plan N with certain conditions, you may see less direct financial benefit from this waiver, since your supplemental plan is already absorbing that cost. For everyone else, the waiver could reduce the temptation to delay or skip a needed checkup simply to avoid an out-of-pocket charge.

sections.text: Will Your Doctor's Visits Qualify? How to Check

sections.content: You don't have to wait until April 2027 to start finding out whether this applies to you. A few simple steps can clarify your situation well ahead of the rollout.

items: Ask your primary care doctor's office directly whether their practice participates in an ACO.
Check your Medicare Summary Notice for any messaging referencing ACO participation or attribution.
Call 1-800-MEDICARE to confirm whether you've been attributed to an ACO based on your claims history.
Watch for official CMS mailings, which typically notify beneficiaries when they're attributed to a participating ACO.

sections.content: If your current doctor is not part of an ACO, you are not required to switch providers to access this benefit. Staying with a doctor you trust is reasonable, even if it means the waiver doesn't apply to your visits yet.

sections.text: What to Watch for Before and After the April 2027 Rollout

sections.content: Participation in the copay waiver is optional for ACOs, meaning not every qualifying practice will adopt it right away, even if they're part of an ACO. Some practices may wait to see how the program works in practice before opting in.

sections.calloutText: CMS guidance on this rule may still change before and after the April 2027 effective date. Confirm current details directly with your doctor's billing office or official CMS sources as the date approaches, rather than assuming the waiver automatically applies.

sections.content: Rather than assuming your visits qualify, ask your doctor's billing office directly closer to the rollout date. They will know whether their ACO has opted into the waiver and how it applies to your specific visits.

It is completely reasonable to take your time understanding this change before deciding anything needs to shift in your coverage. Nothing about this rule requires an immediate decision, since it doesn't take effect until April 2027.

When you're ready, a licensed Medicare agent can review your specific situation, including checking whether your doctor participates in a qualifying ACO, without pushing you toward a plan change. Comparing your current Medicare coverage against this update can help clarify whether any adjustments actually make sense for your budget and your care needs, or whether your current setup already works well for you.

faqs.question: I'd rather read more before talking to anyone about this change. Is that okay?
faqs.answer: Yes. The rule doesn't take effect until April 2027, so there's no need to rush into a conversation before you're ready. Bookmark official CMS updates and this guide so you can check back as more details become available closer to the rollout.

faqs.question: If I call to ask about this, will I get a pushy sales pitch?
faqs.answer: A licensed agent can answer factual questions about your doctor's ACO status and how the waiver might apply without pressuring you to switch plans. A trustworthy resource explains your options clearly and lets you decide on your own timeline, with no obligation to make changes on the call.

faqs.question: How do I know if I can just figure this out myself by reading more?
faqs.answer: Many people prefer researching independently, and that's a reasonable approach for this topic. Checking your Medicare Summary Notice for ACO-related messaging and asking your doctor's office directly whether they participate in an ACO are both simple, self-service first steps you can take right now.

faqs.question: How can I trust that information about this new rule is accurate?
faqs.answer: Cross-check any claims about this rule against official announcements on CMS.gov, since CMS guidance can be updated as the effective date approaches. Licensed MedicareFAQ agents also stay current on CMS rule changes and can confirm details specific to your coverage and your doctor's participation.

sections.text: Your Next Step as This Rule Takes Shape

sections.content: The most useful thing you can do right now is find out whether your primary care doctor participates in an ACO. That single answer tells you whether this waiver is even relevant to your situation once it takes effect.

As CMS publishes final guidance closer to April 2027, it's worth revisiting your coverage to see how the details apply to your specific visits and costs. When you're ready, speaking with a licensed agent is a low-pressure way to understand how this change fits into your overall Medicare coverage, on your own schedule.
